citation.authors: Lianmin Zheng, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ying Sheng, Siyuan Zhuang, Zhanghao Wu, Yonghao Zhuang, Zi Lin, Zhuohan Li, Dacheng Li, Eric P. Xing, Hao Zhang, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Ion Stoica
citation.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
citation.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks (37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)

fetched_urls: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.05685 (v4, 24 Dec 2023; read pages 1-9 of the PDF directly)

claims.planned: Catalogues judge biases: position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias, limited reasoning/math grading ability — confirm each with the paper's evidence
claims.finding: Section 3.3 catalogues exactly these four limitations. Evidence: (1) Position bias — Table 2 shows all judges favor positions; most favor first position. (2) Verbosity bias — 'repetitive list' attack on 23 MT-bench answers: failure rates Claude-v1 91.3%, GPT-3.5 91.3%, GPT-4 8.7% (Table 3). (3) Self-enhancement bias — examined statistically: GPT-4 favors itself with a 10% higher win rate, Claude-v1 with 25% higher, but GPT-3.5 does not favor itself; the paper explicitly says results are INCONCLUSIVE. (4) Limited math/reasoning grading — GPT-4 makes incorrect judgments even on elementary math problems it can solve when shown wrong answers; Table 4: 14/20 failure rate on 10 math questions with the default prompt.
claims.quote: We examine the usage and limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, as well as limited reasoning ability... [3.3] Position bias is when an LLM exhibits a propensity to favor certain positions over others... Verbosity bias is when an LLM judge favors longer, verbose responses, even if they are not as clear, high-quality, or accurate as shorter alternatives... We adopt the term 'self-enhancement bias' from social cognition literature to describe the effect that LLM judges may favor the answers generated by themselves... Limited capability in grading math and reasoning questions... it also shows limitations in grading basic math problems which it is capable of solving... It's worth noting that although GPT-4 can solve the problem (when asked separately), it was misled by the provided answers, ultimately resulting in incorrect judgment.

claims.planned: GPT-4 judge agreement with human preferences exceeds 80%, comparable to human-human agreement (~81%?) — confirm exact numbers and how agreement was defined
claims.finding: Confirmed with exact numbers. On MT-bench under setup S2 (non-tie votes only, random baseline R=50%), GPT-4 (pairwise) vs. human agreement is 85% on first turn — exceeding human-human agreement of 81% (first turn; 82% second turn). On Chatbot Arena S2, GPT-4 vs. human agreement is 87%. Definition: agreement = 'the probability of randomly selected individuals (but not identical) of each type agreeing on a randomly selected question.' Two setups: S1 includes non-tie, tie, and inconsistent votes (counts inconsistent as tie; random baseline 33%); S2 only non-tie votes (random baseline 50%).
claims.quote: We define the agreement between two types of judges as the probability of randomly selected individuals (but not identical) of each type agreeing on a randomly selected question... The agreement under setup S2 (w/o tie) between GPT-4 and humans reaches 85%, which is even higher than the agreement among humans (81%). This means GPT-4's judgments closely align with the majority of humans... strong LLM judges like GPT-4 can match both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences well, achieving over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans.

claims.planned: Position bias measurement: judges favor first position; confirm reported consistency numbers
claims.finding: Confirmed via Table 2 (two near-identical GPT-3.5 answers per first-turn question). Consistency (same verdict after swapping order): Claude-v1 23.8% (default prompt) / 56.2% (rename prompt); GPT-3.5 46.2% / 51.2%; GPT-4 65.0% / 66.2%. Bias direction: Claude-v1 biased toward first 75.0% (default); GPT-3.5 biased toward first 50.0%; GPT-4 biased toward first 30.0% vs. second 5.0%. Caveat: 'Most LLM judges favor the first position' — not all; Claude-v1 also shows a name bias toward 'Assistant A' under the rename prompt (biased toward second 28.7%).
claims.quote: As in Table 2, we found all of them exhibit strong position bias. Most LLM judges favor the first position. Claude-v1 also shows a name bias which makes it favors 'Assistant A'... The position bias can be very significant. Only GPT-4 outputs consistent results in more than 60% of cases.

claims.planned: Mitigations proposed: swapping positions, few-shot, chain-of-thought, reference-guided grading
claims.finding: All four confirmed in Section 3.4, plus a fifth (fine-tuning a Vicuna-13B judge, Appendix F). Swapping positions: call judge twice with orders swapped, declare a win only if preferred in both orders, else tie (the 'conservative' approach used in their experiments). Few-shot judge: raises GPT-4 position-bias consistency from 65.0% to 77.5%, but makes API calls 4x more expensive and may introduce new biases, so zero-shot is the default. Chain-of-thought helps math grading (failure rate 14/20 -> 6/20) but the judge often makes 'exactly the same mistake as the given answers'; reference-guided grading (generate the judge's own answer first, show it as reference) cuts failure rate from 70% to 15% (14/20 -> 3/20, Table 4).
claims.quote: Swapping positions. The position bias can be addressed by simple solutions. A conservative approach is to call a judge twice by swapping the order of two answers and only declare a win when an answer is preferred in both orders... the few-shot judge can significantly increase the consistency of GPT-4 from 65.0% to 77.5%... even with the CoT prompt, we find that in many cases LLM makes exactly the same mistake as the given answers... Hence, we propose a reference-guided method... In Table 4, we see a significant improvement in failure rate (from 70% to 15%) over the default prompt.

claims.planned: MT-Bench is 80 multi-turn questions across 8 categories; Chatbot Arena crowdsourced battles
claims.finding: Confirmed. MT-bench: 80 high-quality multi-turn questions (each with 2 turns), 8 categories with 10 manually designed questions each: writing, roleplay, extraction, reasoning, math, coding, knowledge I (STEM), knowledge II (humanities/social science). Chatbot Arena: crowdsourcing platform with anonymous battles — users converse with two anonymous models simultaneously, vote for the preferred response, identities disclosed post-voting; ~30K votes collected after running for one month. Released data: 80 MT-bench questions, 3K expert votes, 30K conversations with human preferences.
claims.quote: We create MT-bench, a benchmark consisting of 80 high-quality multi-turn questions... We identify 8 common categories of user prompts to guide its construction: writing, roleplay, extraction, reasoning, math, coding, knowledge I (STEM), and knowledge II (humanities/social science). For each category, we then manually designed 10 multi-turn questions... Our second approach is Chatbot Arena, a crowdsourcing benchmark platform featuring anonymous battles... After running Chatbot Arena for one month, we have collected around 30K votes.

teachable_points.point: Three LLM-as-a-judge variations with explicit tradeoffs: pairwise comparison (doesn't scale — possible pairs grow quadratically), single answer grading (scalable but absolute scores fluctuate more if the judge model changes), and reference-guided grading.
teachable_points.quote: the pairwise comparison may lack scalability when the number of players increases, given that the number of possible pairs grows quadratically; single answer grading may be unable to discern subtle differences between specific pairs, and its results may become unstable, as absolute scores are likely to fluctuate more than relative pairwise results if the judge model changes.
teachable_points.numbers: GPT-4 single-answer grading agreement with humans: 85% (MT-bench S2, first turn) vs. 85% for pairwise — nearly identical, so the scalable method works.

teachable_points.point: Judge-human agreement is not uniform: it increases with the performance gap between the compared models. When models are close in quality, agreement drops toward 70%; when far apart, it approaches 100%. Course implication: judge reliability depends on how hard the discrimination task is.
teachable_points.quote: we observe the agreement between GPT-4 and human progressively increases in line with the performance disparity of the model pairs (i.e., larger win rate difference), from 70% to nearly 100%.
teachable_points.numbers: 70% to nearly 100% agreement as win-rate difference grows (Figure 2).

teachable_points.point: GPT-4's judgments can change human minds: when a human's choice deviated from GPT-4, showing them GPT-4's judgment led humans to deem it reasonable most of the time and frequently switch their vote.
teachable_points.quote: humans deemed GPT-4's judgments reasonable in 75% of cases and are even willing to change their choices in 34% of cases.

teachable_points.point: The agreement metric design matters: two setups with different random baselines. S1 includes tie/inconsistent votes (random baseline R=33%); S2 excludes ties (R=50%). The headline 85% vs. 81% numbers are S2. Reporting agreement without the baseline is misleading.
teachable_points.quote: 'S1' includes non-tie, tie, and inconsistent (due to position bias) votes and counts inconsistent as tie; 'S2' only includes non-tie votes.
teachable_points.numbers: S1 R=33%, S2 R=50%; MT-bench first turn S1: G4-Pair vs Human 66%, S2: 85%; Human-Human S1: 63%, S2: 81%.

teachable_points.point: Multi-turn judging design: breaking a two-turn conversation into two separate judge prompts causes referencing failures; displaying both complete conversations in a single prompt and asking the judge to focus on the second question alleviates this.
teachable_points.quote: Our finding is the former one can cause the LLM judge struggling to locate the assistant's previous response precisely... We then consider the alternative design that presents two full conversations in a single prompt in which we ask the LLM judge to focus on the second question... This approach has been found to significantly alleviate the aforementioned referencing issue.
teachable_points.numbers: MT-bench: every question has 2 turns, so a pairwise comparison involves 2 questions and 4 responses.

teachable_points.point: Study scale and setup, useful for teaching what 'controlled' vs 'in the wild' human data looks like: MT-bench used 6 models and 58 expert-level human labelers (~3K votes); Arena analysis sampled 3K single-turn votes from 30K, from 2114 unique IPs.
teachable_points.quote: We then use 2 kinds of judges: LLM judges and 58 expert-level human labelers... We randomly sample 3K single-turn votes from 30K arena data... collected crowd judges (2114 unique IPs).
teachable_points.numbers: 6 models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude-V1, Vicuna-13B, Alpaca-13B, LLaMA-13B) on MT-bench; 58 expert labelers; ~3K MT-bench votes; 3K of 30K arena votes; 2114 unique IPs.

teachable_points.point: Calibration detail for the verbosity attack: all judges correctly tie identical answers, but two of three fail the repetitive-list attack — a clean example of a targeted adversarial probe for a specific bias.
teachable_points.quote: As a calibration, we find LLM judges are able to correctly judge identical answers (i.e., they always return a tie for two identical answers) but cannot pass the more advanced 'repetitive list' attack.
teachable_points.numbers: Failure rates on 23 answers: Claude-v1 91.3%, GPT-3.5 91.3%, GPT-4 8.7%.

misconceptions_to_avoid: Do NOT claim the paper proved self-enhancement bias. It explicitly states: 'Due to limited data and small differences, our study cannot determine whether the models exhibit a self-enhancement bias.' GPT-4 favored itself by +10% win rate and Claude-v1 by +25%, but GPT-3.5 did not favor itself, and they note judges also favor other models. The paper catalogues it as a potential limitation, with suggestive-but-inconclusive evidence.

Position bias is 'most judges favor the first position,' not 'all judges always favor first.' Claude-v1 under the 'rename' prompt shows a NAME bias toward 'Assistant A' (28.7% biased toward second position when names are changed), and GPT-4 is biased toward first only 30% of the time (consistent 65%).

The 80%+ agreement headline is the S2 setup (non-tie votes only, 50% random baseline). Under S1 (ties included, 33% baseline) the numbers are lower (e.g., 66% GPT-4-human, 63% human-human on MT-bench first turn). Quote agreement numbers with their setup.
MT-Bench's '80 questions' are first-turn prompts each paired with a second turn (160 total turns: 'an average score of 160 = 80 x 2 turns'). Don't describe it as 80 single prompts.

The chain-of-thought mitigation only partially works for math grading (14/20 -> 6/20 failures); the judge often reproduces the same mistake from the displayed answers. Reference-guided grading is the stronger fix (3/20).
notes_for_authors: Primary source fully verified from the arXiv v4 PDF (24 Dec 2023). This is the canonical LLM-as-a-judge paper and all five planned claims hold, with two nuances worth surfacing in the course: (1) self-enhancement bias is presented as inconclusive — a nice meta-lesson on honest reporting of weak evidence; (2) the agreement metric has two setups with different chance baselines, a perfect concrete example of measurement-definition sensitivity for a course on eval validity. The Table 2 position-bias numbers (Claude-v1 23.8% consistency, GPT-4 65.0%) and Table 3 verbosity attack (91.3%/91.3%/8.7%) are vivid, quotable evidence. Note the paper studies GPT-4 (March 2023 era), GPT-3.5, and Claude-v1 as judges — findings about specific consistency numbers are model-vintage-specific even though the bias taxonomy generalizes. Released artifacts: 80 questions, 3K expert votes, 30K conversations at https://github.com/lm-sys/FastChat/tree/main/fastchat/llm_judge.
